## Round 1 — Authors' Response

We thank the Reviewer for their positive comments on our study and manuscript, and trust that our new data sufficiently reinforces our mechanistic findings and conclusions regarding the role of ASC in contributing to PDAC.
Major comments
1) Is metabolic reprogramming needed to support ASC-dependent malignant cell proliferation?
Author response:
We appreciate the Reviewer’s insightful comment which is based on our in vivo data (in the KPC PDAC mouse model) demonstrating that ASC-mediated pancreatic tumourigenesis (incorporating augmented cellular proliferation in the pancreatic epithelium) is associated with metabolic reprogramming. Given the brevity of this comment, we have assumed that the Reviewer is now requesting in vitro data (consistent with their other comments below). Accordingly, we have performed experimentation with two widely-used transformed human PDAC cell lines, PANC-1 and MIA PaCa-2, whereby we have knocked-down ASC (encoded by PYCARD) with siRNA (ASCKD). As shown in the new Supplementary Figures S14a-h, successful siRNA-mediated knockdown of ASC expression (along with the expected reduced cleaved Caspase-1 levels) significantly reduced cell proliferation, colony formation and viability coincident with reduced lactate levels and increased mitochondrial DNA copy number and gene expression in human PDAC cells. This is consistent with our in vivo data (e.g. Figures 4a, 5i, 7, 8c-g) that genetic ablation of ASC in KPC mice reduced cellular proliferation within the pancreatic epithelium which associated with elevated mitochondrial gene networks and DNA copy number, and a reversion of energy metabolism from aerobic glycolysis (as seen in cancer cells; Warburg effect) towards mitochondrial respiration (as seen in non-cancerous (wild-type) mice with normal, lowly-proliferating cells).
To further assess whether metabolic reprogramming in PDAC cells aligns with ASC-mediated cell proliferation and/or viability, we next treated ASCKD and control (scramble siRNA) transfected PANC-1 and MIA PaCa-2 cells with two glycolysis inhibitors, STF-31 and 2-deoxyglucose (2-DG), noting that cancer cells heavily rely on aerobic glycolysis for proliferation and viability (survival). In contrast to negative control (scramble siRNA) transfected PDAC cells, ASCKD PDAC cells were markedly less sensitive to impaired viability (proliferation) induced by glycolysis inhibitors (Supplementary Figure S14j), which supports the notion that ASC deficiency switches the cellular energy needs for viability and proliferation towards OXPHOS (i.e. mitochondrial respiration).
While being mindful of the Reviewer’s comment below to shorten the Discussion, we have briefly referred to these new human cell line data in the Discussion on pages 19 (lines 443-447) and 21 of (lines 483-485), as well as in the Results (pages 17-18, lines 393-414, 419-422) and Methods (pages 26-27, lines 602-631, 788, 794-796, 802-803) sections.
2) Are oxygen consumption and extracellular acidification rates modulated by ASC in malignant cells?
Author response:
A key finding of our study was that ASC-containing inflammasomes promoted mitochondrial dysfunction resulting in a bias towards aerobic glycolysis (Warburg effect) in PDAC, as evidenced by the blockade of ASC (in the KPC PDAC model) which switched energy metabolism back towards mitochondrial-driven OXPHOS (i.e. cellular respiration). To address this comment by the Reviewer, we have therefore performed the Seahorse XF Mito Stress Test to measure key parameters of mitochondrial respiration (oxygen consumption rate; OCR) in the above human PDAC cells subjected to siRNA-mediated knockdown of ASC (ASCKD).
As shown in the new Supplementary Figures 14k and l, both basal OCR and maximal OCR capacity (induced by the proton ionophore FCCP, a potent uncoupler of mitochondrial OXPHOS) were increased in ASCKD versus control (scramble siRNA) transfected human PDAC cells, which further supports our notion that ASC deficiency during PDAC (e.g. in KPC:ASCKO mice) rewires energy metabolism back towards mitochondrial respiration. Furthermore, the spare respiratory capacity (SRC) of ASCKD PDAC cells was also elevated versus control PDAC transfected cells (Supplementary Figures 14k and l), indicating that ASC deficiency enhanced mitochondrial fitness in response to energy demands. We also refer to our new above-mentioned data (in response to comment #1) showing that extracellular lactate production – which is a primary source of extracellular acidification during glycolysis – was significantly reduced in PDAC cells upon siRNA-mediated knockdown of ASC (Supplementary Figure 14h). Collectively, these data indicate that oxygen consumption and extracellular acidification rates are indeed modulated by ASC in transformed (pancreatic) cancer cells.
These new data are now briefly referred to in the Discussion (lines 483-485) on page 21, as well as in the Results (page 18, lines 414-422) and Methods (page 35, lines 821-829) sections.
3) Does extracellular ASC control OXPHOS and glycolysis?
Author response:
In line with the above comments by the Reviewer referring to “malignant cells”, we assume here the Reviewer is also referring to the context of human PDAC cells. Therefore, to address this comment, we have treated human PDAC cells with an ASC-specific nanobody (VHH ) and performed assays for lactate production which (as mentioned above) is an indicator of glycolysis (versus OXPHOS). We note that these experiments were performed with a limiting amount of available human-specific ASC nanobody (VHH ) which is different to the murine ASC (VHH ) used in our study on KPC mice because i) VHH is specific for mouse only ASC, and ii) VHH is specific for human only ASC (also see new text in the Results on page 13, lines 298-301 referring to this - in response to Minor comment #4 by Reviewer #2).
As shown in the figure below for the Reviewer, these experiments (n = 3; each experiment comprising technical triplicates is coded with a specific colour) revealed that VHH reduced lactate production (albeit not significantly; P = 0.0665, paired t-test) which is consistent with our new in vitro data (Supplementary Figure 14) showing that ASC modulates mitochondrial OXPHOS and glycolysis. The observation that the reduction in lactate production in human PDAC cells upon VHH treatment was not as pronounced as that seen in siRNA-mediated knockdown of ASC is analogous to the in vivo situation where the suppressed PDAC phenotype in VHH -treated KPC mice was not as pronounced as that observed upon whole-body ASC deletion in KPC:ASCKO mice (e.g. compare Figure 6d and Supplementary Figure 5e). This could be explained, at least in part, by the global blockade of intracellular and extracellular ASC activity (KPC:ASCKO mice, ASCKD PDAC cells) versus the nanobody-mediated blockade of (predominantly) extracellular ASC activity: note, we have now included new text in the Discussion on page 24, lines 561-565 referring to this). One must also consider that differences in the bioactivity of VHH versus VHH may account for any differential effects observed on mouse versus human cells with these nanobodies. Since these data are preliminary and subject to our ongoing detailed characterization of the mechanisms of action of ASC-targeted nanobodies in cancer, we believe it best to include these data for the Reviewers only.

Our laboratory has housed ASCKO mice under specific pathogen-free (SPF) conditions for nearly 10 years, and we have not encountered any adverse effects (such as an increase in bacterial infections), which is consistent with many other laboratories worldwide who house these mice in SPF facilities. Similarly, we have not encountered any unexpected susceptibility to infections in KPC:ASCKO mice, or for that matter KPC:ASCfl/fl mice, housed in our SPF facility for 4 years and 2 years, respectively (we note that the original ASCfl/fl mice were generated over 10 years ago – see reference 24 – and again have been used worldwide without any health issues). It is widely known and acknowledged that modulation of inflammasome activity does not impact on susceptibility to bacterial infection because of the functional redundancy that exists among the many PRRs (including those associated with inflammasomes) that constitute the innate immune system’s role in host defence against infection. For instance, in ASCKO mice engineered for the functional absence of inflammasome complexes comprising a PRR that recognizes bacterial components, other PRRs (such as those belonging to the Toll-like receptor family) can still recognize and respond to bacteria, thus minimising risk of infection. As requested by the Reviewer, in the Methods section under the subsection “Mice”, we have now added a brief sentence (page 25, lines 589-591 referring to the absence of microbial-driven adverse events (increased susceptibility to bacterial infections) in mice lacking ASC.

Importantly, we point out our new in vitro data generated from human PDAC (i.e. tumour epithelial) cells in response to comments by Reviewer #1. Here, the siRNA-driven targeting of ASC (PYCARD) in these cancer cells directly modulated numerous intrinsic cellular processes comparable to our observations in KPC mice upon genetic ablation of ASC, including: i) reduced cell proliferation and viability, ii) reduced lactate production and increased mitochondrial respiration/oxygen consumption rate (indicative of a switch from glycolysis towards OXPHOS for energy metabolism), iii) increased mtDNA copy number and iv) reduced oxidate stress (i.e. mitochondrial superoxide production) (new Supplementary Figure S14). Moreover, in relation to the Reviewer’s comment, we show in the new Supplementary Figure S14g that siRNA-mediated knockdown of ASC in human PDAC cells directly increased mRNA expression levels of mitochondrial- and nuclear-encoded genes. Taken together with our existing Opal multiplex immunofluorescence analyses (Figures 8h,i, Supplementary Figures S11-S13) which provides spatial context for the predominant localization of ASC-containing inflammasomes with mitochondrial markers in the pancreatic ductal epithelium, we believe these data provide compelling evidence for ASC-mediated tumour (cancer) cell specific effects during PDAC.
In further response to this Reviewer’s comment, firstly we note that a health issue arising with aged (~20-week-old (wo)) KPC mice is the appearance of anogenital and facial warts because of the “leakiness” of the Pdx1-Cre allele which can lead to activation of mutant-Kras in other tissues. As a consequence of this, over the last 6 months we have been directed by our University Veterinarian and Animal Ethics Committee to perform studies on KPC mouse strains only aged up to 12 weeks, so we are currently unable to generate 20wo mice. Secondly, cell sorting for tumour cells is suboptimal because i) spatial context within the TME (of the pancreas) is lost, and ii) in the absence of a highly specific and robust tumour/ductal epithelial cell marker (i.e. antibody) it cannot be assumed that a generic epithelial-specific antibody alone for sorting will capture only tumour cells. For these reasons, we are currently undertaking a combinatorial approach of spatial transcriptomics (archived 12wo and 20wo mouse FFPE pancreas samples) coupled with single-cell RNASeq (fresh 12wo) on WT, KPC, KPC:ASCKO and KPC:ASCfl/fl mice to align the expression of mitochondrial- and nuclear-encoded ASC-dependent genes and molecular pathways to distinct cellular compartments (i.e. tumour/ductal epithelial cells, acinar cells, immune cell subsets, fibroblasts etc) within pancreatic lesions. As the Reviewer can appreciate, this is quite an undertaking and is well beyond the scope of the current study: we envisage our ongoing combinatorial transcriptomics studies will form the basis of a future independent manuscript.

4. Nanobody Specificity: More data or citation supporting the specificity of VHHASC for extracellular ASC specks in vivo would strengthen the therapeutic relevance and rule out off-target effects.

We refer the Reviewer to two cited publications (manuscript references 21 and 31) by co-authors Bernardo Franklin and Florian Schmidt who have previously demonstrated the specificity of the ASC nanobody (VHH ) in blocking the activities of extracellular ASC specks in vitro and in vivo. For example, in reference 31 (e.g. Figure 1, Schmidt FI et al. J Exp Med), experimental data are presented whereby recombinant VHH (targeting human ASC) is used to immunoprecipitate a single specific band of ASC from cell lysates, and fluorescently labelled VHH specifically stains ASC specks. These and other data in this study by Schmidt et al verify the high degree of specificity of VHH against (human) ASC. More recently, experimental data presented in reference 21 (e.g. Figure EV3, Bertheloot D et al. EMBO Mol Med) show that VHH (targeting murine ASC – used in our current study) specifically binds to mouse ASC (via its pyrin domain), but not to human ASC or the pyrin domain of other inflammasome components (e.g. NLRP3). Moreover, Bertheloot et al (e.g. Figures 4 and EV4) demonstrate that VHH blocks the pro‐inflammatory functions of extracellular ASC specks and predominantly targets ASC specks in the extracellular space. Importantly, we also note that no off-targets effects have been observed in vivo with VHH in inflammatory disease models (i.e. gout and arthritis, see Figures 6 and 7 in Bertheloot et al), similar to our own current observations in the KPC PDAC model.
In line with the comments by the Reviewer, we have now modified the text and added a statement in the Results section on page 13 (lines 298-301) of the revised manuscript emphasizing the specificity of VHH against extracellular ASC specks and the absence of any known off-target effects.
5. PRR Partner for ASC: Although the Discussion mentions the uncertainty regarding the PRR responsible for ASC inflammasome activation in PDAC, no experiments or strong hypotheses are proposed. Even correlative analysis of PRR expression in epithelial vs. immune compartments would be informative.
Author response:
As the Reviewer can appreciate, the discovery of the ASC inflammasome-associated PRR(s) that promotes PDAC is a significant undertaking that is beyond the scope of this current manuscript, and in fact constitutes a major study being performed in our laboratory at present. In this regard, to screen for ASC-interacting PRR(s) that promote PDAC, we have performed a proteomics-based approach, termed Rapid Immunoprecipitation Mass Spectrometry of Endogenous Protein (RIME), on pancreatic tissues from the KPC mouse model (and appropriate controls including WT and ASC-deficient KPC mice) at defined time points. RIME is a robust proteomics strategy that is used to identify protein-protein interactions, including previously by our laboratory (Balic JJ et al, Oncogene; PMID 31481496). Having identified several candidate ASC-interacting PRRs, we are currently performing validation studies that include genetic targeting of each candidate in KPC mice, along with correlative expression (mRNA, protein) analyses in different cellular compartments within the TME of KPC mice and clinical biopsies and datasets. Therefore, we strongly believe it would be prematurely speculative and potentially compromise novelty of our ongoing studies (and subsequent manuscript(s)) to include such correlative analyses in our current study.
Importantly, we refer the Reviewer to existing data presented in main Figure 2a,b and Supplementary Figure 2d showing the expression profile of numerous inflammasome-associated PRRs in pancreatic tumours from KPC mice and PDAC patients, respectively. These data demonstrate that upregulation of several inflammasome-associated PRRs in pancreatic tumours aligns with that observed for ASC (and Caspase-1). To address the Reviewer’s comment, while being mindful to shorten the Discussion (see comment by Reviewer #1), we have briefly added new text in the Discussion section on page 22 (lines 545-547) which refers to our current experimental strategy (RIME) to identify the PRR(s) responsible for ASC inflammasome activation in PDAC.
